title: Correlated Subqueries and EXISTS
description: Understand correlated subqueries that reference the outer query, and learn when to use EXISTS and NOT EXISTS for efficient existence checks.

data.text: A correlated subquery is a subquery that depends on the outer query — it references a column from the outer query inside its own WHERE clause. Unlike a regular subquery that runs once, a correlated subquery is re-evaluated for every row the outer query processes.

data.title: Performance warning
data.text: A correlated subquery over N rows executes N times. On large tables this can be painfully slow. Always check whether a JOIN or a CTE can express the same logic more efficiently.
Find products whose list price equals the highest price in their own category. The subquery references p1.category_id from the outer query:

data.title: Correlated subquery finding max price per category
data.code:
SELECT product_name, list_price, category_id
FROM   production.products p1
WHERE  list_price = (
    SELECT MAX(list_price)
    FROM   production.products p2
    WHERE  p2.category_id = p1.category_id
)
ORDER BY category_id, product_name;

data.text: The EXISTS operator tests whether a subquery returns *any* rows at all. It returns TRUE as soon as it finds the first matching row — it does not care about the actual values, only whether rows exist. This makes it ideal for existence checks and it naturally pairs with correlated subqueries.

data.title: EXISTS — find customers who placed orders in 2017
data.code:
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, city
FROM   sales.customers c
WHERE  EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM   sales.orders o
    WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND  YEAR(order_date) = 2017
)
ORDER BY first_name, last_name;

data.title: SELECT 1 vs SELECT * in EXISTS
data.text: Inside EXISTS, use SELECT 1 (or SELECT NULL) rather than SELECT *. Since EXISTS only checks for row existence, the column list is irrelevant — SELECT 1 avoids the overhead of building a result set.
NOT EXISTS is perfect for finding 'orphans' — rows in one table that have no matching row in another. This is often called an 'anti-join.'

data.title: Customers who never placed an order
data.code:
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name
FROM   sales.customers c
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM   sales.orders o
    WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
ORDER BY first_name;

data.text: For existence checks, EXISTS, IN, and JOIN can often produce the same result. The choice matters for both correctness and performance:

rows: You need to check existence and don't need columns from the subquery
The subquery returns a small, known set; or you are comparing to a literal list
You need columns from the related table in the output

data.title: NULLs and IN
data.text: IN (subquery) returns UNKNOWN (not TRUE) if the subquery contains a NULL. NOT IN returns FALSE for every row when NULLs are present. EXISTS does not have this problem — it is NULL-safe.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query and re-runs for every outer row
EXISTS returns TRUE as soon as the subquery yields any row; use SELECT 1 for clarity
NOT EXISTS is the standard pattern for finding orphaned (unmatched) rows
IN with a subquery containing NULLs can silently filter out everything — prefer EXISTS for safety
Correlated subqueries can be slow on large datasets; consider JOINs or CTEs instead
